newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Pro-government parties head Moroccan vote-count.
newsitem.headline: Pro-government parties head Moroccan vote-count.

text.p: Pro-government and centre-right parties dominated early results in Morocco's local elections on Saturday after a poll which will help shape a powerful new Upper House of parliament later this year.

"The preliminary results showed that the four-party Koutla (opposition bloc) won 7,532 seats out of a total 24,253 in the communal and municipal councils," Interior Minister Driss Basri told reporters.
Another small opposition group, the Socialist Democratic Party, took 138 seats while independent candidates won 2,364 seats, Basri said.
The remaining majority seats were held by eight pro-government parties led by the Independent National Rally (RNI), he said.

The elections were contested by a dozen parties, most of them linked up in three alliances -- the opposition Koutla, the pro-government rightist Wifaq group and a centre-right group led by the Independent National Rally.
An average 74.8 percent of the electorate of around 13 million had turned out to vote on Friday, he added.
The final results are expected before 1700 GMT, the interior ministry said.
The old guard Istiqlal party, one of the four making up the Koutla, had taken the largest number of seats, a total of 4,062, the interior ministry said.
On Saturday, the Istiqlal party paper l'Opinion said: "The operation of the vote in certain areas was marked by irregularities, as was the case during the electoral campaign."
The second largest party to emerge from the partial results was the RNI with 3,430.
The local elections for 1,547 councils are the first of a series due to culminate in September with a general election for a new lower house of parliament.

Under the constitution, a new Upper House is to be formed with power to topple the government through a no-confidence motion, with 60 percent of its members being chosen by the local councils emerging from Friday's ballot.
Al-Maghrib newspaper on Saturday termed Friday's ballot "an essential step on the way to strengthening local democracy for the economic and social development of all the kingdom's regions."

Results had been expected earlier with polling booths closing at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT) on Friday. But senior officials in hundreds of stations used their prerogative under the law to stay open for a further two hours to give more voters chance to cast ballots.

Opposition parties had campaigned strongly to try to change three decades of rule at all levels by pro-government parties after King Hassan said on television last year that he was fed up with vote-rigging charges and personally pledged honest elections.
Under planned decentralisation, regional councils will also have more money and power to push development projects to end the disparity between town and country.
About half of the population of 28 million live in the countryside and have higher illiteracy rates, poorer health and lower living standards than people in the cities.
Pro-government and centre-right parties won about two-thirds of the seats in a 1992 ballot.
